transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

My family says I’m always getting sidetracked and forgetting what I was supposed to be doing. They've started worrying that I might be having some memory problems, so I promised them I'd come in to get it checked out.
Can you tell me more about getting sidetracked, does it happen often and in what kinds of situations, like at work, school, or during daily chores?

Yes, it happens very frequently now when I'm trying to do chores around the house. For example, I’ll go to the shed or start cooking, but then a bird outside the window or a passing thought pulls me away, and I end up leaving things half-finished. This has really become a major, noticeable issue over the past year since I retired and took on more commitments.
Do you also find yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or having trouble waiting for your turn in lines or when doing quiet activities, in addition to getting sidetracked easily?

Yes, I definitely feel restless inside, especially during long meetings at the community center or in waiting rooms where I'm constantly shifting in my seat and looking for an excuse to stand up. I also struggle with quiet activities like reading or meditation because my legs get fidgety and my mind starts wandering, so I usually end up getting up to tinker with something instead.

Do you often find yourself interrupting others during conversations, blurting out answers before questions have been completed, or intruding on conversations, and if so, how frequently does this happen?
No, I don't really have that problem of interrupting or blurting things out. If anything, I tend to quiet down or zone out during conversations rather than intruding on others.
Have you experienced any significant distress, anxiety, or feelings of overwhelm related to your symptoms of getting sidetracked, restlessness, or difficulty with quiet activities?

Yes, I get really overwhelmed trying to coordinate my commitments and not knowing where to start, which made my family and me worry that this was early dementia. It's also very frustrating to feel so internally restless when I just want to sit quietly and relax.

Can you describe how these symptoms of getting sidetracked, restlessness, and difficulty with quiet activities have affected your daily life, relationships, or overall well-being, and have you noticed any significant changes in your mood or interest in activities you once enjoyed?

Lately, I’ve been double-booking myself and missing appointments, which has caused my wife and kids to lose some trust in me and stop asking for my help. I haven't noticed any changes in my mood or interest, though, as I still feel sharp and really enjoy my DIY workshops and card games when I'm engaged—the struggle is just staying organized and on track.

Can you tell me at what age you first noticed these symptoms of inattention and restlessness, and have they been present throughout your life or did they start more recently, perhaps around the time of your retirement?

While these issues have become much more of a problem over the past year since I retired, they actually go all the way back to my childhood. Even in primary school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was always daydreaming, missing instructions, and forgetting to bring home the right books. It's something I've lived with my whole life, but it has just gotten much harder to manage lately with more commitments.
Did you experience significant hyperactivity, such as running, climbing, or being constantly on the go, during your childhood, or was it more about inattention and restlessness?

As a child, it was definitely more about daydreaming and inattention rather than physical hyperactivity like running or climbing. In primary school, my teachers often told my parents that I was missing instructions and forgetting my books, though I could answer their questions just fine once they actually got my attention.

Now that you're an adult, do you find yourself often feeling the need to be on the go, or do you exhibit other signs of physical hyperactivity, such as tapping hands or feet, or leaving your seat in situations where you're expected to remain seated?

While I don't run around wildly, I do experience a strong sense of internal restlessness and physical fidgetiness. During long meetings or in waiting rooms, I feel a constant urge to shift in my seat and look for excuses to stand up or walk to the hallway. Even when trying to sit quietly, my legs get so fidgety that I usually have to get up and tinker with something.
Have you ever been told or noticed that you have difficulty engaging in leisure activities quietly, such as reading or doing puzzles, due to feeling restless or a need to be active?

Yes, I definitely have that difficulty. I like the idea of sitting and reading or doing quiet meditation at the senior center, but after just a few minutes my legs get fidgety and my mind starts wandering. I usually end up turning on the radio or getting up to tinker with something instead.

Can you think of any situations, either currently or in the past, where you exhibited more overt signs of hyperactivity, such as excessive running, climbing, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, which might have been more pronounced than just feeling restless or fidgety?

No, I don't recall ever having those kinds of overt physical behaviors like running around or climbing excessively, even when I was younger. For me, it has always been more about an internal sense of restlessness and having fidgety legs. I just find it very hard to sit through quiet activities without needing to shift around, stand up, or find something to tinker with.

You've mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood but have become more challenging to manage since your retirement. Can you tell me how these symptoms have specifically impacted your daily functioning and relationships, and have you noticed any periods where your symptoms improved or worsened significantly?

Lately, these issues have caused me to double-book myself, miss appointments, and let down my family and the senior center, which has made my wife and kids lose trust in me and stop asking for my help. They became significantly worse and really stood out over the past year, right after I retired and tried to take on more responsibilities.

Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where you felt completely free of these symptoms of inattention, restlessness, and difficulty with quiet activities, or have they been consistently present, albeit with varying degrees of severity?

No, I've never really been completely free of them; they have been pretty consistent throughout my life. Even back in primary school, I was always daydreaming and forgetting my books, but I managed to get by. It's only since retiring and taking on so many loose commitments without a fixed routine that these issues have really spiraled into a major problem.
Have you noticed any significant differences in how your symptoms affect you in structured versus unstructured environments, such as at work versus during retirement?

Yes, shifting away from a fixed routine after retirement has made my symptoms much more noticeable. I now loosely structure my days around social and volunteer activities rather than a set schedule, and taking on more of these unstructured commitments over the past year has left me feeling overwhelmed, getting sidetracked, and missing appointments.

You mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood but have worsened since retirement. Can you clarify if you experienced any significant improvement in your symptoms during your adult life, particularly during periods of high structure, such as when you were working, before they worsened again after retirement?

I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't thought about it deeply, but I think I always had some struggles. It's possible the strict routine of my working years masked the issues slightly and kept me on track. Now that I don't have that daily structure, everything has just become much more obvious.

Can you compare how your symptoms of inattention and restlessness were managed and perceived by you and others during your working years versus after retirement, considering the change in structure and responsibilities?

During my working years, the fixed daily routine kept me on track, so my struggles were much less disruptive and I managed to get by. Since retiring, especially over the past year with so many unstructured volunteer tasks, my sidetracking, missed dates, and restlessness have become much more obvious. It’s this sudden lack of structure that made my family start worrying about my memory, whereas before I was able to handle it.

You've mentioned feeling restless and fidgety, but can you tell me if you've ever exhibited any signs of hyperactivity that interfered with your social, occupational, or other areas of functioning, such as excessive talking, feeling constantly on the go, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, and if so, how this has impacted your daily life?

I wouldn't say I'm hyperactive in a loud way, but I definitely struggle to stay still and quiet, constantly shifting during long meetings or failing to sit through meditation because my legs get so fidgety. This makes participating in quiet community activities very hard for me, as I always have to get up to tinker with something. However, the biggest impact on my daily life and family trust has still been from the forgetting and double-booking rather than the restlessness itself.

Can you think of any specific situations, either currently or in the past, where you might have exhibited more overt signs of hyperactivity, such as excessive talking, feeling an intense need to be on the go, or having difficulty engaging in quiet leisure activities without getting restless, which could help differentiate between the possible diagnoses?

I don't really see myself as an overly talkative or hyperactive person, but I definitely experience a lot of internal restlessness and struggle with quiet activities. When I try to do quiet meditation or reading at the senior center, my legs get very fidgety and my mind wanders, so I usually end up getting up to tinker with something instead. During long meetings or in waiting rooms, I also feel that constant inner urge to shift in my seat and look for any excuse to stand up.
Have you ever felt like you were constantly on the go or had an inability to engage in quiet leisure activities without feeling restless, even when you were younger or in different environments?

I’ve never really felt "constantly on the go" like a motor, but I definitely struggle with quiet activities. Whenever I try to sit still to read or meditate, my legs get fidgety and my mind wanders, so I usually end up getting up to tinker with something. Even in waiting rooms or long meetings, I get this internal restlessness where I have to constantly shift in my seat and look for an excuse to stand up.

Can you describe how the severity of your symptoms, such as inattention and restlessness, has impacted your ability to maintain relationships, employment, or daily responsibilities, and have you noticed any significant differences in how these symptoms affect you in different settings or at different times in your life?

Because I constantly double-book myself and miss appointments, my wife and kids have lost some trust in me and stopped asking me for help. While these issues actually go back to primary school when teachers said I daydreamed and missed instructions, they became much more problematic over the past year after I retired and took on more unstructured commitments.

Can you rate the overall severity of your symptoms, such as inattention and restlessness, on a scale from 1 to 10, with 1 being mild and 10 being severe, and how have you seen this severity impact your daily life and relationships over time?

I would probably rate it around a 3 or 4 out of 10 because it feels relatively mild overall, but it still has a very significant impact on my life. It has led to me double-booking myself, missing appointments, and letting down my family and senior center commitments. The most painful part of all this is that my wife and kids have lost some trust in me and have stopped asking me to help with certain things.
Have you ever felt like you had to be constantly moving or doing something with your hands, even in situations where it might not be appropriate, and if so, can you give me some examples?

I don't necessarily feel a need to constantly move my hands, but I do get very fidgety legs and a strong inner restlessness. For instance, during long meetings or in waiting rooms, I constantly shift in my seat and look for any excuse to stand up and walk to the hallway. If I try to sit quietly to read or meditate, my legs get so restless that I have to get up and tinker with something instead.
Have you ever experienced periods where you felt an intense urge to engage in physical activity, such as running or exercising, as a way to relieve your feelings of restlessness?

No, I don't really feel an intense urge to run or do heavy exercise to burn off energy. Instead, it's more of a general fidgetiness where I just feel the need to shift in my seat, stand up and walk around, or find something to tinker with.

Can you recall any instances where you exhibited overt signs of hyperactivity, such as excessive running, climbing, or being constantly on the go, which might have been more pronounced than just feeling restless or fidgety, especially during your childhood or adolescence?

No, I didn't have those kinds of overt physical behaviors like running or climbing when I was young. Back in school, my difficulties were much more about daydreaming, missing instructions, and forgetting to bring home the right books. It was always about my mind drifting off rather than being physically hyperactive.
Have you ever been told by others that you appear overly active or restless, even when you don't feel like you're being hyperactive, and if so, how often does this happen?

I don't recall anyone specifically telling me that I look overly active or restless. I certainly feel restless and fidgety on the inside quite a bit, but I'm really not sure how often other people actually notice it.

Can you think of any situations where you might have exhibited more noticeable signs of hyperactivity, such as feeling an intense need to be on the go, that could help clarify the severity of your symptoms?

I don't really experience that "on the go" feeling, but I do have a strong sense of inner restlessness. During long meetings or in waiting rooms, I get very fidgety, constantly shifting in my seat and looking for an excuse to stand up. I also struggle with quiet activities like reading or meditation because my legs get restless and I feel compelled to get up and tinker with something instead.

Can you think of any instances where you had to be constantly active, such as excessive running, climbing, or an inability to play quietly, which might have been noticeable to others, especially during your childhood or when you were in highly structured environments?

I don't recall having those specific hyperactive behaviors like excessive running or climbing as a child. I really don't think that was ever an issue for me back then. My struggles at that age were always much more about daydreaming and losing focus.

Can you recall any specific situations, either as a child or an adult, where you felt like you were unable to control your physical activity or had to be constantly moving, even in situations where it was not appropriate?

No, I've never felt like I couldn't control myself or had to be constantly moving. For me, it is just that internal restlessness where my legs get very fidgety during long meetings or quiet activities, making me feel a strong urge to shift around or get up to tinker with something.

Looking back, did you ever have any periods in your life where you felt like your restlessness and fidgetiness significantly improved or were much less noticeable, perhaps during times of high structure or routine, and if so, what were you doing differently during those times?

I'm not really sure, and I can't recall any specific period in my life where the restlessness and fidgetiness actually went away. Before I retired, having a regular work routine definitely kept me busy, but I don't remember if it truly made those restless feelings improve.

Can you think of any situations where you might have exhibited more overt signs of hyperactivity, such as excessive talking or feeling an intense need to be on the go, that could help differentiate between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive type, and other unspecified attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder?

I don't really talk excessively or feel like I am constantly "on the go" like a motor. However, I do experience a strong inner restlessness, and during long meetings or when waiting, I feel a constant urge to shift in my seat, stand up, or walk around. I also find it very hard to engage in quiet activities like reading or meditating without my legs getting fidgety and needing to get up and tinker with something.
